question: An operations lead must give all staff a one-page summary of a new expense policy. The full twenty-page policy document is open on her screen. What should she do first?
options: A) Ask for a friendly one-page summary now, and attach the policy document only if the first result looks wrong.
B) Paste the policy text itself into the request, so the summary is built from the wording staff will be held to.
C) Type out the handful of policy points she remembers as important, and ask Claude to expand each of them.
D) Ask Claude what expense rules organisations of a similar size normally apply, and adapt that answer for staff.
correct_answers: B) Paste the policy text itself into the request, so the summary is built from the wording staff will be held to.
explanations: She has no way to tell whether the first result is wrong without the policy in front of Claude, because a fluent summary of the wrong content still reads well.

Correct. The source material has to be in the request before anything useful can be written from it. Pasting the actual policy is what makes the summary reflect the rules staff are accountable to, rather than a plausible-sounding approximation.
Working from memory reintroduces exactly the errors a summary is meant to remove, and it silently narrows the summary to the points she happened to recall.
General practice at comparable organisations is not this organisation's policy. Staff will be held to the document, and a summary built from typical rules will differ from it in ways nobody catches.
